text: USS Nina was a United States Navy steamer commissioned in 1866 and served in multiple roles, including as a tug, torpedo boat, torpedo boat tender, salvage ship, supply ship, and submarine tender, before sinking in a storm in 1910. She was a fourth-rate iron-hulled screw steamer laid down by Reaney, Son & Archbold at Chester, Pennsylvania, in 1864, launched on 27 May 1865, and delivered at the New York Navy Yard in Brooklyn, New York, on 26 September 1865. She was placed in service as a yard tug at the Washington Navy Yard in Washington, D.C., on 6 January 1866, under Ensign F. C. Hall, alongside the tugs USS Primrose and USS Rescue. Nina operated as a yard tug at the Washington Navy Yard and Naval Gun Factory through May 1869, then was converted into a torpedo boat and recommissioned on 31 March 1870, departing for Newport, Rhode Island, where she arrived on 14 April 1870 and served as a torpedo boat through 1883. In May 1884, she was refitted for special service and operated from August to October 1884 salvaging the wreck of sidewheel gunboat USS Tallapoosa, which had sunk in Vineyard Sound off the coast of Massachusetts. From 1885 to 1889, she served at the New York Navy Yard, then operated at Newport from 1890 to 1891. On 12 March 1891, Nina departed the New York Navy Yard with the decommissioned armed steamer USS Galena in tow for the Portsmouth Navy Yard in Kittery, Maine, where Galena was to be fitted with new boilers. On 13 March 1891, both ships ran aground in fog on a beach about 1 mile (1.6 km) south of Gay Head on Martha's Vineyard off the coast of Massachusetts. Both were refloated a few days later; Galena was deemed beyond economical repair, but Nina was repaired and returned to service. In 1892, she was reassigned to the New York Navy Yard to resume her original duties, continuing yard work and towing services there for a decade. On 8 October 1902, she was recommissioned as a torpedo boat tender and supply ship for the Torpedo Boat Flotilla during winter maneuvers in the Caribbean. She returned to the New York Navy Yard on 15 March 1903 and was decommissioned on 21 March 1903, resuming yard towing duties. She was next loaned to the Lighthouse Department to verify aids to navigation near Puerto Rican waters to protect the fleet during winter maneuvers from October 1903 to April 1904. She was recommissioned on 9 September 1905 for special service with the Board of Inspection and Survey at Rockland, Maine. On 28 December 1905, Nina was ordered converted into a submarine tender. On 25 May 1906, she arrived at the Naval Torpedo Station at Newport and, after a year’s service, was assigned as torpedo boat tender for the 1st Torpedo Flotilla. For the next four years, she served with the United States Atlantic Fleet’s infant submarine force in pioneering coastal operations along the U.S. East Coast from Newport to Annapolis, Maryland, and Norfolk, Virginia. From 1 December 1908 to 22 February 1909, she participated in the great naval review in Hampton Roads, Virginia, following the return of the Great White Fleet from its around-the-world cruise and joined submarines in exercises off the coast of Virginia. At 0630 on 6 February 1910, Nina departed Norfolk bound for Boston, Massachusetts, and was last sighted off the Capes of the Chesapeake in the midst of a gale. She was never heard from again and was declared lost and struck from the Navy List on 15 March 1910, with the 30 crewmen and one officer on board listed as having died on that day. In 1978, divers discovered her wreck in the Atlantic Ocean, 11 nautical miles (20 km; 13 mi) northeast of Ocean City, Maryland, in 90 feet (27 m) of water.
